questions.q: What did the study find about river nitrate?
options: Wet climates flush nitrate downstream, leaving the highest levels in tropical rivers
Rivers in forested mountain regions hold almost no nitrate because of heavy rainfall
Dry climates are associated with high nitrate even with little farming or urban development
Nitrate pollution has fallen worldwide since stricter farm regulations were introduced
questions.explain: Scarce water lets natural nitrate accumulate rather than be diluted.

questions.q: How many monitoring sites supplied data?
options: More than 7,000
Fewer than 700
Roughly 37,000
Over 2.9 million
questions.explain: They combined measurements from more than 7,000 monitoring sites.

questions.q: What common sources of nitrate are mentioned at the start?
options: Industrial discharges, mining runoff and coastal spills
Runoff from farm fields, sewage systems and cities
Leaching from soils, wetlands and natural groundwater
Stormwater, road salt and urban landscaping runoff
questions.explain: The passage begins by listing runoff from farm fields, sewage systems and cities as typical nitrate sources.

questions.q: Why are small headwater streams important?
options: They are well monitored and rarely contain nitrate above the 2.5 mg/L level
They dilute nitrate from farms before it reaches larger rivers downstream
They can accumulate nitrate under low flow and feed larger drinking-water rivers
They are too small to hold nitrate, so they are excluded from global maps
questions.explain: They often cease to flow, concentrate nitrate, and feed larger rivers.

questions.q: What does the author imply about a warming world?
options: Wetter regions will see rising nitrate as runoff from storms increases
Treatment plants will remove nitrate as temperatures and river flows rise
Drier regions may see rising nitrate even without added nitrogen
Nitrate levels will fall as rivers warm and microbes consume more of it
questions.explain: They ask how much nitrate will rise if regions become drier even without added nitrogen.
